title: "Skill Demand and Supply in Poland 2025"
subtitle: "Insights from Online Job Postings and Trainings"
date: today

## Executive Summary

::: {.hero}
```{=html}
<div class="hero-title">Executive Summary</div>
```

This report provides an evidence-based assessment of skill demand and
training supply in Poland in 2025, combining large-scale online
job-posting data from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>
with training-service data from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR)</a>.
The analysis treats online vacancies as a timely proxy for employer demand
and BUR listings as a proxy for the publicly visible, subsidised training
supply. Both sources are transformed into comparable skill measures using
NLP methods and mapped mainly to the ESCO taxonomy, with Lightcast used
to capture more granular AI-related skill signals. The focus is
compositional: the report compares the distribution of skills demanded
by employers with the distribution of skills supplied through training,
rather than attempting to compare the absolute number of vacancies with
the number of training participants.

The main finding is that Poland's training supply only partially matches
the structure of employer demand. Employer demand is concentrated in
management, communication, collaboration, digital, ICT, and
business-administration skills. BUR training provision, by contrast, is
relatively more concentrated in assisting and caring, machinery-related,
services, health, and welfare skills. The resulting mismatch is moderate
at the broad ESCO pillar level and more substantial at the more granular
sub-group level, suggesting that the policy challenge is not only to
expand training provision but to reallocate part of the training
portfolio toward the skills most demanded in market-based hiring.

Digital and AI skills emerge as central areas of demand. Among classified
digital skill mentions, advanced digital skills account for the largest
share, followed by basic and intermediate skills. This suggests that
digitalisation in Poland is not limited to basic ICT adoption; many
employers are already seeking higher-order digital capabilities.
AI-related demand remains small in total job postings under a conservative
matching approach, but it is concentrated in knowledge-intensive services,
especially professional, scientific, technical, telecommunications, IT,
and information services. This pattern points to an early-stage but
strategically important AI labour market, where demand is still narrow but
likely to be important for productivity growth and competitiveness.

Green skills are present but still moderate in scale. Regional green-skill
demand varies within a relatively narrow range, while sectoral intensity
is highest in utilities, energy, agriculture, and public administration.
In absolute terms, however, green demand is largest in large-employment
sectors such as trade, professional services, and manufacturing. This
distinction is important for policy: sector-specific green transition
strategies should target high-intensity sectors, but large-scale upskilling
efforts should also account for sectors where green skills are less
concentrated but affect many workers.

The report also highlights the importance of migration and care-related
labour needs. Postings explicitly tagged as open to Ukrainian workers are
concentrated in hospitality, transport, manufacturing, food retail,
restaurants, warehousing, and manual or operational roles. Their regional
distribution appears to reflect sectoral structure and refugee settlement
geography more than overall labour-market tightness. In care and
public-health training, Pracuj.pl captures only a narrow part of direct care
demand, while BUR shows a growing but still small public-health training
segment. This reinforces the need to interpret demand–supply comparisons
carefully where either source has known coverage limitations.

For policymakers, the results support three priorities. First, strengthen
the alignment of subsidised training with employer demand in management,
digital, ICT, business, and transversal skills. Second, maintain targeted
support for care, health, and inclusion-related training, while recognising
that online vacancies understate demand in public and social services.
Third, develop more granular labour-market intelligence systems that
combine online vacancy data, training registries, administrative sources,
and taxonomies such as ESCO and Lightcast. Such systems can help Poland
move from retrospective monitoring toward faster, evidence-based skill
policy.
:::

## Data Coverage

::: {.section-card}
### Data collection

We collect job advertisements from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>,
the largest online job portal in Poland, and training-service listings
from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych</a>,
the country's main public database of training and upskilling services.
The analytical sample shown in this report focuses on records that can
be assigned to Polish voivodeships and linked to the regional demand and
supply comparison.

For job advertisements, we retain records with sufficient textual
content to support downstream NLP processing, including job titles and
descriptions. For BUR, we use training-service records with usable
regional metadata and service descriptions. We remove duplicates and
standardize core fields before the records enter the analytical
pipeline.


## Methodology

::: {.section-card}
### Processing pipeline

Raw job postings and training descriptions contain noisy, unstructured
information in Polish (and occasionally English or other languages). We
transform them into a standardised analytic dataset in six steps: we
first identify the source language, translate non-Polish text into
Polish, isolate skill-relevant sentences, map extracted skills to the
ESCO and Lightcast skill taxonomies, standardise job titles to ESCO
occupations using both titles and skill context for disambiguation, and
then enrich each record with sector codes and regional information for
voivodeship-level comparison.

::: {.section-card}
### Digital Skill Levels in Poland

Using the classification proposed by
<span class="paper-ref" data-tooltip="Chinen, M., and Montorsi, C. 2025. Exploring Digital Skills Demand: Key Insights from Online Job Vacancies in South Africa, Nigeria, Kenya, and Uganda. Education Working Paper No. 21. Washington, DC: World Bank."><a class="paper-link" href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099746512082541920/pdf/IDU-dcae1207-ed6e-4383-9c7f-1f2b2dbae522.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Chinen &amp; Montorsi (2025)</a></span>,
we group ESCO-linked digital skills into `basic`, `intermediate`, and
`advanced` categories. Across Poland, 696,092 digital skill mentions
from job postings can be classified in this way. The resulting profile
shows that advanced digital skills account for the largest share of
classified digital demand.


### AI Skills Demand

The demand for AI-related skills is highly dynamic, with new
technologies and tools emerging rapidly while others become obsolete.
This makes it difficult to track AI skill demand using static
taxonomies alone.

Lightcast captures highly granular and technology-specific signals, such
as individual AI tools, models, copilots, libraries, and chatbot
platforms. This makes it well suited to detecting early changes in
employer demand. We start from a benchmark of **350 AI skills from
Lightcast** used by
<span class="paper-ref" data-tooltip="Martins-Neto, A., Liu, Y., Khurana, S., and Porras Lopez, J. M. 2026. Click, Code, Earn: The Returns to Digital Skills. World Bank."><a class="paper-link" href="https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/099451102172652767/pdf/IDU-e779b9af-e9b1-43ae-a2c5-9679dbf2d829.pdf" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Martins-Neto et al. (2026)</a></span>
and extend it with 114 additional skills that have since appeared in the
Lightcast taxonomy, bringing the current total to 464 AI skills.

To make the full list policy-readable, we organize these 464 skills into
four primary categories and eight cross-cutting tags. The primary
categories are mutually exclusive and capture the fundamental domain of
each skill. The tags are non-exclusive and highlight secondary
dimensions that cut across categories.

```{=html}
<div class="ai-category-grid" id="ai-category-cards"></div>
<div id="ai-tag-chart"></div>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Lightcast AI skills taxonomy; Martins-Neto et al. (2026); authors' categorization.</p>
```
:::

### Green Skills Demand

::: {.section-card}
#### Identification approach

Green skills are identified by matching the ESCO skills extracted from
job postings (Step 04 of the pipeline) against the official
<a class="paper-link" href="https://esco.ec.europa.eu/en/about-esco/publications/publication/green-skills-and-knowledge-concepts-labelling-esco" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">ESCO Green Skills and Knowledge Collection<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>,
a curated subset of roughly 830 skills and knowledge concepts that the
European Commission classifies as relevant to the green transition.

A job posting is counted as "green" if at least one of its matched ESCO
skills belongs to this collection. Because the ESCO green taxonomy is
broad and includes some entries that are only tangentially related to
environmental sustainability, we apply a manual review step: each
matched skill is classified as either **genuine green** or **false
positive** based on whether its presence in a job posting plausibly
signals demand for environmental or sustainability competences.

```{=html}
<div class="kpi-grid" id="green-kpi-cards"></div>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}

#### False positives

Not all skills in the ESCO green collection carry a clear environmental
signal when they appear in Polish job postings. Skills such as *building
codes*, *vehicle type-approval*, or *warehouse management software* are
part of the ESCO green taxonomy but frequently appear in postings where
the role has no meaningful green dimension. After matching, we manually
flag these as false positives and exclude them from the headline green
skill counts. The full list of excluded skills is shown below.

```{=html}
<details class="green-fp-details">
  <summary>Show excluded false-positive skills (click to expand)</summary>
  <div class="data-table-wrap" id="green-false-positives-list"></div>
</details>
```
:::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Regional green skill demand

The map shows the share of job postings with at least one genuine green
skill in each voivodeship. Regional variation is moderate: shares range
from roughly 2.5% to 4.0%, with higher concentrations in voivodeships
where construction, energy, and agricultural sectors are more prominent.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 32.</strong> Share of job postings with at least one green skill, by voivodeship</div>
<div id="green-regional-map"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Green-skill demand varies moderately across regions, with higher shares in areas linked to construction, energy, and agriculture. Regional green policies should therefore account for local industrial structure.</p>
<div class="map-caption source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl job postings; ESCO Green Skills Collection; authors' matching and manual review.</div>
```
:::::

::: {.section-card}
#### Most demanded green skills

The chart below shows the 25 most frequently demanded genuine green
skills across all job postings. Environmental engineering, environmental
management standards, and the design of heating and cooling systems lead
the ranking, reflecting Poland's strong construction and energy
infrastructure sectors.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 33.</strong> Top 25 genuine green skills by number of job offers</div>
<div id="green-top-skills-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> The leading green skills are linked to environmental engineering, environmental management, and heating/cooling systems. This points to practical green-transition demand in construction, energy infrastructure, and environmental compliance.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl job postings; ESCO Green Skills Collection; authors' matching and manual review.</p>
```
:::

{{< include includes/wb_results_green_nace.qmd >}}

::: {.section-card}
#### Top occupations by green skill demand

The chart ranks the 15 KZIS (Polish Classification of Occupations)
occupations with the highest number of job postings containing at least
one genuine green skill. Sales representatives appear at the top partly
because of the large volume of postings in that occupation, but the
green-skill content of these offers points clearly to specific segments:
above all renewable energy and energy-efficiency sales, green building
solutions, and agri-related product markets. The most common green
skills for this occupation include promoting sustainability, advising on
the energy efficiency of heating systems, installing photovoltaic
systems, energy efficiency, agronomy, and the energy performance of
buildings. Specialised roles such as environmental engineers and
environmental protection specialists show higher average green skill
intensity per posting.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 35.</strong> Top 15 KZIS occupations by number of offers with green skills</div>
<div id="green-top-occupations-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Green demand is not limited to specialist environmental roles; high-volume occupations such as sales representatives also carry green-skill signals. This suggests that green transition skills are diffusing into commercial and client-facing occupations.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl job postings; ESCO Green Skills Collection; KZIS occupation matches; authors' matching and manual review.</p>
```

### Jobs for Ukrainians

::: {.section-card}
#### Background

Polish job postings on Pracuj.pl can carry an explicit
**Запрошуємо працівників з України / Jobs for Ukrainians** badge, added by
the employer to signal that the role is open to (and the workplace is
prepared to support) Ukrainian candidates. The tag was introduced
shortly after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022
as part of Pracuj.pl's response to the wave of refugees arriving in
Poland — see
<a class="paper-link" href="https://media.pracuj.pl/179412-grupa-pracuj-dla-ukrainy" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Grupa Pracuj dla Ukrainy<span class="source-link-ext">↗</span></a>.

We retrieve the badge by parsing the `data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"`
HTML element on each posting's detail page, and join the result back to
the structured fields in `job_ads`. Looking at where this tag appears
tells us which **regions, industries and occupations** are most actively
opening up to workers from Ukraine — and by extension, to foreign labour
more broadly. It also reveals where employer demand and refugee supply
overlap most strongly.

```{=html}
<div class="kpi-grid" id="ukr-kpi-cards"></div>
```
:::

::::: {.section-card .map-shell}
#### Regional intensity

The map shows the share of all 2025 Pracuj.pl postings in each
voivodeship that carry the Jobs-for-Ukrainians tag. Małopolskie leads
clearly (around 14% of postings), followed by Lubuskie, Łódzkie,
Lubelskie and Dolnośląskie — a mix of regions with large refugee
populations (Małopolskie, Dolnośląskie), border-area logistics hubs and
food-processing clusters (Lubuskie, Lubelskie, Łódzkie). Mazowieckie has
the largest absolute number of tagged offers but a lower share, since
its labour market is dominated by professional and IT roles where the
tag is less commonly used.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 36.</strong> Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship (2025)</div>
<div id="ukr-regional-map"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Ukrainian-friendly postings are regionally uneven, with Małopolskie standing out. The pattern likely reflects refugee settlement geography and sectoral composition rather than general labour-market tightness alone.</p>
<div class="map-caption source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings with <code>data-test="sections-benefit-ukrainian-friendly"</code>; authors' parsing.</div>
```
:::::

::: {.section-card}
#### Demand intensity vs Ukrainian-friendly share

A natural question is whether voivodeships with a **hotter labour
market** — measured as total job offers per 100k labour force — are also
the ones where employers more often choose to **flag a posting as
Ukrainian-friendly**. Plotting the within-region share (Y, %) against
total offer intensity (X) gives a much weaker relationship than one
might expect: across the 16 voivodeships, **Pearson r ≈ +0.24**,
**Spearman ρ ≈ +0.26**, **R² ≈ 0.06**. In other words, demand intensity
explains very little of the cross-regional variation in how often the
badge is used.

The clearest outlier is **Małopolskie**, sitting well above the cloud at
≈14% of postings tagged despite only mid-range overall intensity — a
likely echo of Kraków's large post-2022 Ukrainian diaspora.
**Kujawsko-Pomorskie** (~6.6%) and **Podkarpackie** (~7.0%) sit clearly
below the cloud, while **Mazowieckie** — by far the densest labour
market — is exactly average on the share dimension (~9.7%). This
suggests the Ukrainian-friendly tag tracks **demographic factors**
(refugee settlement patterns) and **sectoral mix** much more than
overall hiring intensity.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 37.</strong> Total offers per 100k labour force vs share of offers tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by voivodeship</div>
<div id="ukr-density-scatter"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> The weak relationship between overall demand intensity and Ukrainian-friendly shares suggests that employers’ openness to Ukrainian workers is driven more by sectoral and demographic factors than by aggregate vacancy pressure.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings; Statistics Poland (BAEL) labour-force averages 2025; authors' computation. Each marker is one of the 16 voivodeships; the dashed line is the OLS fit.</p>
```
:::

### Beyond the voivodeship map — decomposing where the tag really comes from

The voivodeship picture above is suggestive but limited. An aggregate map
cannot tell whether a local gap in Ukrainian-friendly hiring is driven by
**what** employers hire for (sectoral mix) or **how** they hire within
those sectors (behaviour). To answer this we apply a shift-share (Oaxaca)
decomposition on **683,104 postings** with a resolved powiat and a NACE
mapping.

```{=html}
<section class="cards" id="ukr-decomp-kpis" aria-label="Decomposition KPIs"></section>
```

::: {.section-card}
#### Shift-share (Oaxaca) decomposition

For every powiat $p$, the deviation of its Ukrainian-friendly share from
the national share can be written exactly as

$$
s_p - s_{PL} \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_k w_{pk}\bigl(s_{pk} - s_{PL,k}\bigr)}_{\text{within-sector (behavioural)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_k \bigl(w_{pk}-w_{PL,k}\bigr) s_{PL,k}}_{\text{between-sector (composition)}}
$$

where $k$ indexes **NACE divisions** (2-digit codes), $w_{pk}$ is the
share of postings in division $k$ within powiat $p$, and $s_{pk}$ is the
local within-division Ukrainian-friendly share. The first term answers:
*"Given the sectors that operate here, how much more (or less) often
does an employer flag the tag than the national norm?"* The second
answers: *"How much of the gap is just due to over- or under-
representation of UA-friendly-prone sectors?"*

```{=html}
<div class="chart-block">
  <div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 38.</strong> Shift-share decomposition of the Ukrainian-friendly gap from the national share — 16 voivodeships</div>
  <div id="ukr-shift-voivodeship" class="plotly-chart" role="img" aria-label="Stacked horizontal bar of within-sector and composition components of UA-tag share gap for 16 voivodeships"></div>
  <p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Małopolskie's +4.8 pp gap is almost entirely behavioural — its sectoral mix accounts for just +0.2 pp; the rest is local employers being more willing to flag the tag. The reverse is true for Mazowieckie, where a slightly positive within-sector signal is dragged below zero by an over-representation of professional / IT roles where the tag is rarely used.</p>
  <p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025); NACE division mapping; authors' computation. Diamonds mark the observed gap = within + between.</p>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="chart-block">
  <div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 39.</strong> Shift-share decomposition — top-20 powiats by |gap|</div>
  <div id="ukr-shift-powiat" class="plotly-chart" role="img" aria-label="Stacked horizontal bar of within-sector and composition components for top-20 powiats"></div>
  <p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Polkowicki's +20.8 pp gap is dominated by the within-sector term (+19.6 pp): even at the same sectoral mix as Poland, local employers there flag the tag far more often. Tatrzański is the clearest "composition" case — about a third of its gap is a hospitality-and-services tilt typical of mountain resorts.</p>
  <p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl postings (2025). Only powiats with ≥ 100 postings are eligible; ranking by absolute gap.</p>
</div>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Industries (NACE sections)

Aggregated to the top-level NACE section, the Ukrainian-friendly tag is
strongly concentrated in service sectors that absorb low-barrier labour:
**accommodation and food service (I)** stands out at roughly a third of
all postings, followed by **transportation and storage (H)** and
**manufacturing (C)**. Sections dominated by professional services and
public administration use the tag much less frequently.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 40.</strong> NACE sections with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-section-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Ukrainian-friendly hiring is concentrated in hospitality, transport, and manufacturing. These sectors often involve operational roles with lower formal credential barriers and higher labour turnover.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Sections shown have at least 5,000 postings.</p>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Industries (NACE divisions)

Drilling down to NACE divisions exposes the specific niches driving
demand for Ukrainian workers. By share, the leaders are food retail and
restaurants (G47.5, G47.22, I56.11, G47.11), passenger road transport
(H49.32, H49.33) and goods road transport (H49.41) — sectors with high
turnover, language-tolerant tasks and a strong refugee employment
footprint. By absolute volume, **restaurants (I56.11)**, **warehousing
(H52.1)** and **programming activities (K62.1)** dominate, the last
reflecting the large pool of Ukrainian IT specialists who relocated
after 2022.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 41.</strong> NACE divisions with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-share-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> At a more detailed sector level, food retail, restaurants, and road transport stand out. These niches are particularly important for refugee and migrant labour-market integration.</p>
<div class="figure-caption-title" style="margin-top:1rem;"><strong>Figure 42.</strong> NACE divisions with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-industries-count-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> In absolute terms, restaurants, warehousing, and programming activities dominate Ukrainian-friendly postings. This shows that both lower-barrier service work and higher-skill IT employment matter for Ukrainian workers in Poland.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl + ESCO→NACE crosswalk. Only divisions with at least 500 postings are ranked.</p>
```
:::

::: {.section-card}
#### Occupational categories

Using Pracuj.pl's own narrow job categories (`job_category_narrow`), the
tag is most prevalent in food-related and manual-labour roles —
*Food products*, *Hospitality staff*, *Manual labour*,
*Couriers / delivery* — and in hospitality and personal-services
categories such as *Hotel operations* and *Hairdresser / beautician*. The
absolute-volume ranking confirms that gastronomy, courier and warehouse
categories together account for the bulk of Ukrainian-friendly hiring.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 43.</strong> Narrow job categories with the highest share of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-categories-narrow-share-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> The tag is most prevalent in food-related, hospitality, manual-labour, courier, and personal-service categories. These are practical entry points for migrant employment policy.</p>
<div class="figure-caption-title" style="margin-top:1rem;"><strong>Figure 44.</strong> Narrow job categories with the largest absolute number of Ukrainian-friendly postings</div>
<div id="ukr-categories-narrow-count-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> High-volume Ukrainian-friendly hiring is concentrated in gastronomy, courier, warehouse, and related operational categories. This identifies where language support, credential recognition, and workplace integration could have the largest reach.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl <code>job_category_narrow</code>. Only categories with at least 500 postings are ranked.</p>
```
:::

{{< include includes/wb_ukr_nace.qmd >}}

::: {.section-card}
#### Seniority and contract types

The tag overwhelmingly attaches to **manual-worker**
roles — over a fifth of such postings are Ukrainian-friendly — and to a
hybrid `manager / supervisor` shift-leader category common in retail and
gastronomy. Specialist, expert and director roles see the tag much
less. On the contract side, **temporary employment contracts** and **contracts of mandate** carry the
tag most often, reflecting the prevalence of short-tenure agency-style
hiring in the segments where Ukrainian workers are most actively
recruited; standard permanent contracts and B2B contracts use the tag
considerably less.

```{=html}
<div class="figure-caption-title"><strong>Figure 46.</strong> Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by seniority level</div>
<div id="ukr-seniority-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Ukrainian-friendly postings are concentrated in manual-worker and supervisor-type roles, while specialist and director roles use the tag less often. This suggests that the badge mainly supports operational rather than high-skill professional recruitment.</p>
<div class="figure-caption-title" style="margin-top:1rem;"><strong>Figure 47.</strong> Share of postings tagged 'Jobs for Ukrainians', by contract type</div>
<div id="ukr-contracts-chart"></div>
<p class="figure-interpretation"><strong>Interpretation.</strong> Temporary and mandate contracts carry the tag more often than permanent or B2B contracts. This points to a relatively flexible and sometimes more precarious employment structure in migrant-accessible segments.</p>
<p class="notes source-note">Source: Pracuj.pl <code>seniority_level</code> and <code>contract_types</code>. Multi-valued fields are split per posting; only categories with at least 500 postings are shown.</p>
```
:::

{{< include includes/wb_care_services.qmd >}}

## Conclusions

::: {.section-card}

This report demonstrates that online labour-market intelligence can provide a timely and granular view of Poland's evolving skills landscape. By combining vacancy data from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://www.pracuj.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Pracuj.pl</a>
with training-service data from
<a class="paper-link" href="https://uslugirozwojowe.parp.gov.pl/" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">Baza Usług Rozwojowych (BUR)</a>,
the analysis offers a structured comparison between the skills employers request and the skills supplied through registered training provision. While neither source should be interpreted as a complete representation of the labour market or the training system, together they provide valuable evidence on the direction of skills demand, the orientation of training supply, and potential areas of misalignment.

The findings suggest that Poland's skills system faces a dual challenge. On the one hand, employers continue to demand a broad set of foundational and transversal skills, including communication, collaboration, management, self-organisation, and business-related competences. These skills are not confined to a single sector or occupation; rather, they underpin productivity across much of the economy. On the other hand, demand for more specialised skills linked to digitalisation, ICT, data use, artificial intelligence, and the green transition is becoming increasingly visible. This combination points to a labour market in which both general employability skills and more advanced technical capabilities are central to future competitiveness.

The comparison with BUR training provision shows that the current training offer only partly reflects this structure of demand. Training supply is relatively more concentrated in care, health, welfare, services, and machinery-related areas, while employer demand is more strongly oriented toward management, business administration, digital, ICT, communication, and teamwork-related skills. This does not mean that the areas emphasised in training supply are unimportant. Many of them respond to genuine social needs, including demographic ageing, health-care pressures, and demand for care-related services. However, the observed differences indicate that training policy may need to more explicitly balance social priorities with the skills required for productivity growth, organisational upgrading, and digital transformation.

Digital skills deserve particular attention. The analysis shows that employer demand is not limited to basic digital literacy. Advanced digital skills constitute a substantial share of classified digital-skill mentions, suggesting that many firms are already seeking capabilities related to data, software, ICT systems, and more complex digital tasks. At the same time, AI-related demand remains relatively concentrated in knowledge-intensive sectors, especially professional, scientific, technical, information, and communication activities. This pattern is consistent with an early stage of diffusion, where AI capabilities are not yet universal but are strategically important for high-productivity segments of the economy. Skills policy should therefore avoid treating AI as a niche technology while also recognising that broad-based AI adoption will require complementary managerial, organisational, and transversal skills.

Green skills show a different pattern. Their regional variation is moderate, but their sectoral concentration is clearer, with stronger intensity in utilities, energy-related activities, agriculture, public administration, and selected technical fields. At the same time, many green-skill mentions appear in larger sectors where the green share is lower but the absolute number of affected workers may be substantial. This distinction matters for policy design. Targeted sectoral interventions are needed in high-intensity green-transition sectors, while broader upskilling efforts should ensure that green competences also reach mainstream occupations in trade, manufacturing, construction, and professional services.

The report also points to the importance of inclusion-oriented skills policy. Job postings explicitly open to Ukrainian workers are concentrated in specific sectors and occupations, including hospitality, transport, manufacturing, warehousing, food services, and selected IT-related roles. This suggests that migrant integration policies should combine general labour-market access measures with sector-specific support, including language training, recognition of prior experience, workplace integration, and pathways from entry-level jobs toward more stable and higher-productivity employment. Similarly, the analysis of care-related work and public-health training highlights the need to interpret online vacancy data in relation to coverage patterns, as some socially important areas of labour demand may be less visible in private job boards than in other administrative or sector-specific sources.

A key methodological conclusion is that no single data source provides a complete view of skills demand and supply. The value of online labour-market data lies in its timeliness, granularity, and rich textual content, but also in the fact that it captures a particular segment of the labour market. In the Polish context, Pracuj.pl provides especially strong coverage of market-based recruitment for white-collar, specialist, managerial, and ICT-related occupations. Official vacancy registers and public employment service data, by contrast, tend to capture a different part of the labour market, including more blue-collar, lower-wage, public-sector, and locally recruited vacancies. These sources should therefore not be treated as competing measures of the same phenomenon, but as complementary windows into different segments of labour demand.

The same logic applies to the supply side. BUR data provide detailed and verified information on registered training services, but they represent only one part of the broader skills supply ecosystem. A fuller assessment of skills provision would require linking BUR data with additional sources, such as curricula from vocational and higher education institutions, adult-learning programmes, sectoral training initiatives, certification schemes, and employer-provided training. Integrating these sources would make it possible to compare not only the skills demanded by employers and advertised by training providers, but also the skills embedded in formal education pathways and other learning opportunities.

A promising next step is therefore to build a more integrated skills intelligence system that combines multiple verified sources with different coverage profiles. Such a system would use online job postings, official vacancy registers, public employment service data, training registries, curricula, and possibly stated preference studies as complementary evidence. Online and administrative data can reveal observed demand and available supply, while stated preference studies can help explain worker and employer choices, constraints, and willingness to participate in training. Together, these sources would provide a more balanced picture of Poland's skills ecosystem and support better-targeted policy decisions.

For Poland, the results support a shift from static training planning toward a more adaptive skills system. Such a system would regularly compare employer demand with training supply, identify emerging skill gaps earlier, and provide evidence for reallocating public funding toward areas with strong economic and social returns. This does not imply that training provision should mechanically follow current vacancies. Public policy must also account for long-term development goals, demographic pressures, regional cohesion, and inclusion. However, systematic skills intelligence can help ensure that these priorities are pursued with a clearer understanding of labour-market needs.

Overall, the analysis suggests that Poland has a substantial opportunity to strengthen the alignment between its training ecosystem and the changing structure of work. Better alignment would require expanding provision in digital, ICT, business, management, and transversal skills, while preserving targeted support for care, health, green transition, and migrant integration.

:::
